tldr: We propose DexSeed, a framework that takes human hand-object interaction data as a few "seeds" and automatically expands them into diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations through geometric retargeting and physics-simulation reinforcement learning. A VLA model fine-tuned purely on the generated data demonstrates zero-shot execution of language-specified grasps on a real multi-fingered robot hand.
hero_caption: Overall concept of DexSeed. Human hand-object interaction data is categorized by grasp mode and automatically expanded in simulation into motion data for a multi-fingered robot hand and arm. A VLA model trained solely on the generated data executes different grasp modes according to language instructions on real-world objects (such as top grasp vs. diagonal wrap grasp on the same apple).
overview:
Dexterous manipulation using multi-fingered robot hands has long been a dream in robotics. Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly generate actions from vision and language have gained significant traction. However, training a VLA for multi-fingered hands requires massive, diverse demonstration datasets featuring coordinated motions across both the arm and numerous fingers. Gathering such data by teleoperating high-DoF hands imposes an immense burden on human operators and fails to scale.

To address this, the authors asked: "Can we reuse abundant existing human hand-object contact datasets and automatically expand them into executable robot data?" The challenge is that human and robot hands differ in morphology, and changes in object geometry or location break contact relationships. Moreover, even when hand shapes are geometrically transferred in simulation, tracking errors at the arm's end-effector during actual arm movement cause the robot to drop the object.

In DexSeed, human grasp sequences are first clustered into "grasp modes" based on similarity and paired with language descriptions. Next, InteractionMesh—which preserves local spatial neighborhood relationships between the hand and the object—is used to retarget motions to the robot hand and new object geometries, followed by expansion into diverse pick-and-place trajectories. The core innovation lies in training a finger residual reinforcement learning (RL) policy under a physics simulation that mirrors real-arm end-effector tracking errors, filtering out only physically viable, successful rollouts as demonstration data. Finally, realistic rendering via 3D Gaussian Splatting is applied to train the VLA.

In experiments, DexSeed automatically generated 25,270 successful demonstrations from just 19 human motion sequences. Without collecting any real-world demonstrations, the VLA fine-tuned solely on this synthetic data achieved high success rates on grasping and placement tasks under specified grasp modes using a real Franka arm and Wuji hand.
contributions: Built "DexSeed", an automated framework that organizes human hand-object interaction data by grasp mode and expands them into diverse robot demonstrations along with language descriptions specifying grasp styles.

Established a data generation pipeline that retargets motions to robot hands and novel object shapes while preserving contact structures via InteractionMesh, and extracts physically executable trajectories using finger residual RL that accounts for arm-tracking dynamics.

Generated 25,270 verified demonstrations from 19 human interaction sequences (across 8 grasp modes), demonstrating that a multi-fingered VLA trained purely on simulation-generated data can execute language-specified grasps on a real robot without real-world demonstration collection.

sections.heading: The bottleneck in multi-fingered data collection and the DexSeed idea
sections.summary: Training dexterous multi-fingered manipulation with VLA models requires vast amounts of robot data, but teleoperation is exceptionally difficult. This paper introduces DexSeed, which automatically generates diverse, physically executable demonstrations at low cost from existing human hand-object interactions.
sections.details:
Controlling dexterous multi-fingered hands is a major goal in robotics research. While VLA models integrating vision, language, and action offer a promising approach, they require large amounts of training data containing coordinated arm and finger motions, visual observations, and language instructions. However, collecting stable grasp demonstrations by teleoperating hands with over 20 degrees of freedom places an extreme burden on human operators and is practically unfeasible at scale.

On the other hand, rich datasets capturing human hand-object contact motions (such as GRAB) already exist. Transferring these to robots could dramatically reduce data collection costs. However, simple geometric shape retargeting is insufficient. Altering object geometries or placement locations breaks local contact relationships. Furthermore, because physical robots experience trajectory-tracking errors in the arm, simply replaying geometrically correct hand poses causes the robot to drop the object.

DexSeed tackles this issue with the following approach. First, human interaction sequences are grouped based on geometric grasp features and paired with GPT-generated grasp descriptions. Next, motions are adapted to the robot hand and novel object geometries using InteractionMesh, which preserves local geometric relationships. Then, finger residual RL is trained while modeling arm lag and tracking errors in simulation, filtering out only trajectories that succeed under real physics. Finally, photorealistic images are rendered using 3D Gaussian Splatting to build a multimodal demonstration dataset for VLA training. From just 19 human seed sequences, DexSeed generated 25,270 executable demonstrations and achieved successful zero-shot transfer to a physical robot.

sections.heading: Lineage of dexterous manipulation data, human-to-robot transfer, and policy learning
sections.summary: The paper surveys three prior lines of research—dexterous data collection, human-to-robot motion transfer, and simulation-based data augmentation for policy learning—and discusses how DexSeed integrates and advances them.
sections.details:
The related work spans three main areas:

### II-A Dexterous Manipulation Data
Data sources for learning dexterous manipulation include human hand-object interaction datasets, direct robot teleoperation, and synthetic data generation systems. Human data captures rich behaviors but lacks robot actions and visual observations, whereas robot teleoperation provides direct actions but is notoriously hard to scale. DexSeed bridges this gap by converting human data into robot-executable demonstrations.

### II-B Human-to-robot Transfer and Physical Realization
Human and robot hands differ in joint count and link lengths. To overcome these morphological differences (cross-embodiment), prior methods optimize joint angles while preserving contact relationships. In particular, methods like InteractionMesh—which model the local spatial hand-object relationship using a Delaunay tetrahedral mesh—effectively preserve contact during pose transfer. Techniques for physically tracking retargeted trajectories in simulation (physics-based imitation and residual control) have also been studied. DexSeed introduces a novel perspective by combining these approaches with RL that accounts for whole-arm tracking dynamics.

### II-C Robot-centric Data Generation for Policy Learning
Recent efforts (such as MimicGen) generate extensive imitation learning datasets by perturbing object placements and trajectories in simulation. Some works, like UniDex, target multi-fingered hands, but they often rely on point cloud inputs or require manual retargeting interventions. DexSeed offers an end-to-end automated framework covering geometric retargeting, whole-arm trajectory augmentation, physical realization, RGB rendering, and language annotation directly from human sequences.

sections.heading: How DexSeed works: from grasp bank clustering to VLA fine-tuning
sections.summary: DexSeed consists of a pipeline encompassing grasp bank construction, InteractionMesh retargeting, arm trajectory expansion, physical execution verification in simulation, realistic rendering, and VLA fine-tuning.
sections.details:
The DexSeed workflow consists of three primary stages: grasp bank construction, data generation, and VLA learning.

### III-A Grasp Bank Construction
From the GRAB human motion dataset, a 170-dimensional feature descriptor is computed at the moment an object begins moving. It concatenates finger flexion angles ($\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{13}$), joint positions relative to the wrist ($\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{63}$), the palm upward vector, vectors from hand joints to the closest object surface points ($\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{63}$), and handle penetration indicators ($\mathbf{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{5}$). Distances between these descriptors are clustered to select 8 representative "grasp modes." Each mode is paired with a shared text description generated via GPT that explains how fingers should be positioned.

### III-B Dexterous Robot Data Generation
- **InteractionMesh Retargeting**: A 3D Delaunay tetrahedral mesh is formed between human hand joints and object surface anchor points to calculate Laplacian coordinates $\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t,i} = \mathbf{v}_{t,i} - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(i)|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}\mathbf{v}_{t,j}$. This characterizes local relative geometries. Poses are optimized for the Wuji hand (20 DoF) and novel object shapes (mapped via Diff3F features) by minimizing the Laplacian difference $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InterMesh}}$.
- **Whole-Arm Trajectory Augmentation**: For each generated grasp and lift motion, random tabletop initial poses and target placement locations are sampled. Approach and place trajectories are spliced together, and joint trajectories for the 7-DoF Franka arm are computed via inverse kinematics (IK).
- **Physics-Based Imitation**: Geometrically solved trajectories fail upon direct replay due to contact slip and arm tracking lag. Using IsaacLab, an RL policy is trained to output residual joint commands for the 20-DoF fingers while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories under PD control. Crucially, the reward function pairs contact maintenance ($R_{\mathrm{contact}}$) and fingertip position ($R_{\mathrm{tip}}$) with an object tracking reward ($R_{\mathrm{obj}}$) that includes a tolerance window matching the arm's end-effector tracking error. Only successful rollouts that complete the task are saved.
- **Photorealistic Rendering**: The physical tabletop environment is reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Successful trajectories are replayed while rendering head and wrist camera views. Random perturbations are applied to lighting, textures, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics to enhance sim-to-real transfer.

### III-C Robot-Centric VLA Learning
Built on the pretrained Lingbot-VLA, the action head is modified to output 27-dimensional actions (7 arm DoF + 20 finger DoF) and fine-tuned on the generated multimodal data. During inference, the policy takes head/wrist images, proprioception, and language grasp descriptions to directly predict coordinated arm and finger actions.

sections.heading: Experiments: retargeting quality, physical realization, and real-robot VLA transfer
sections.summary: The retargeting accuracy, simulation tracking success, and simulation pick-and-place VLA success of DexSeed were benchmarked against baselines. Furthermore, the VLA trained purely on simulation data was deployed on a real Franka arm and Wuji hand, successfully performing instructed grasp modes.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
From the GRAB dataset, 19 sequences across 8 grasp modes (G1–G8) were selected, yielding 25,270 successful trajectories. The robot setup consists of a Franka arm (7 DoF) and a Wuji hand (20 DoF). LingBot-VLA was fine-tuned for 55,000 steps across 8 H20 GPUs.

### IV-B Interaction Retargeting Comparison
DexSeed was evaluated against Dex-Retargeting, SPIDER, and the official Wuji retargeter. DexSeed outperformed all baselines in fingertip contact distance error, contact angle error, and penetration depth. It adapted well to altered object geometries—such as bananas, mugs, and scaled tori—without disrupting contact relationships.

### IV-C Physics-Based Imitation Evaluation
Prior methods like ManipTrans and Dexplore assume a floating hand. When mounted on an arm (FR3), arm tracking delay severely worsened object tracking error, causing success rates to drop. In contrast, DexSeed trains with arm dynamics, allowing fingers to make real-time residual adjustments under end-effector tracking errors. This yielded high contact recall and task success. An ablation trained without the arm (w/o Arm) showed noticeable degradation, underscoring the necessity of keeping the arm in the RL training loop.

### IV-D Simulation VLA Learning Evaluation
Pick-and-place performance was evaluated under four settings of increasing difficulty: Seen, Unseen Locations (Unseen L), Unseen Geometries (Unseen G), and Unseen Appearances (Unseen A). DexSeed VLA significantly outperformed physical imitation baselines (ManipTrans, Dexplore) and unverified kinematic data. Removing geometric augmentation caused performance to drop on unseen shapes; removing appearance augmentation hurt unseen appearance generalization; and removing grasp mode text descriptions reduced overall success. Conditioning on different grasp descriptions for the same apple successfully produced distinct, intended finger joint configurations.

### IV-E Real-World Deployment and Limitations
Deploying on the real Franka arm and Wuji hand across the 8 grasp modes, the policy succeeded in picking and placing objects across all modes without collecting any real-world demonstrations. Performance saw a slight drop in modes requiring sub-centimeter alignment, such as threading a finger through a mug handle (G5: Handle threading), but overall practical efficacy was confirmed.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: DexSeed is a powerful framework that expands a small seed of human hand-object interactions into diverse, physically executable multi-fingered robot demonstrations. Having achieved successful real-robot transfer using purely synthetic data, future directions include in-hand manipulation and bimanual tasks.
sections.details:
This paper introduced DexSeed, a framework that generates language-conditioned dexterous manipulation demonstrations from human hand-object interaction sequences. By uniting grasp-mode data organization, InteractionMesh geometric retargeting, RL physical realization under arm dynamics, and photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, the method scales high-quality robot data.

Experiments confirmed that a VLA fine-tuned solely on this generated data executes multi-fingered grasping and placement in the physical world without requiring any real-world demonstrations.

Future research directions include addressing in-hand manipulation—such as reorienting or repositioning objects within the grasp after picking—and extending the framework to bimanual tasks where one hand stabilizes an object while the other manipulates it. Furthermore, incorporating tactile sensor signals into both the data generation pipeline and the VLA policy could enable dynamic grasp force adjustment upon detecting slippage.

takeaways: Teleoperating multi-fingered hands is extremely difficult, but using existing human hand-object datasets (like GRAB) as "seeds" allows affordable, massive generation of high-quality robot demonstrations.
Geometrically retargeting poses is not enough; training residual finger RL that mirrors arm tracking delay in simulation is essential for extracting physically executable demonstrations.
Pairing photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering with appearance domain randomization enables zero-shot real-robot deployment of multi-fingered VLAs trained entirely on simulation data.
limitations: Tasks are primarily restricted to pick-and-place; in-hand manipulation (such as rolling or regrasping an object inside the palm) is not supported.
Real-world success drops on grasp modes requiring millimeter-level precision, such as threading a finger through a mug handle.
The policy relies solely on vision and proprioception, lacking integration of tactile feedback to detect slippage and dynamically tighten the grip.
